content: Uncomplicated urinary tract infection (UTI) is the most common bacterial infection affecting women. It is primarily characterized by symptoms such as painful urination (dysuria) and an increased frequency of urination. In some countries, urinary alkalisers are commonly used as a treatment option to alleviate these symptoms. Additionally, certain national formularies recommend their use. However, there is currently insufficient empirical evidence to support the effectiveness of urinary alkalisers in treating UTIs. In fact, some healthcare guidelines explicitly advise against their use. The objective of this study was to evaluate both the potential benefits and harms associated with the use of urinary alkalisers in the treatment of uncomplicated UTIs in adult women. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted using the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialised Register up to January 19, 2016. The search was performed in collaboration with the Trials Search Coordinator, employing terms relevant to the topic under review. The inclusion criteria for this review encompassed all randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that investigated the use of any type of urinary alkaliser, either as a standalone treatment or in combination with other therapies, for the symptomatic management of uncomplicated UTIs in women aged 16 years and older. Eligible studies included those where the diagnosis of UTI was based on symptoms alone, a positive urine dipstick test, or urine culture. Studies involving patients with recurrent UTIs were also included, provided that the patients had been symptom-free for at least two weeks prior to the onset of the current symptoms that prompted them to seek medical care. However, studies were excluded if they involved patients with complicated UTIs, immune-compromising conditions, acute pyelonephritis, or chronic conditions such as interstitial cystitis. The process of data collection and analysis involved three authors independently assessing and screening the identified studies. This process was repeated by two additional authors independently, with a third investigator serving as an arbitrator in cases of disagreement. Despite these efforts, no studies met the inclusion criteria for this review, and as a result, no data extraction was performed. The search process initially identified 172 potential studies for inclusion. However, upon detailed assessment, none of these studies fulfilled the predefined inclusion criteria. Consequently, no evidence was available to evaluate the safety or efficacy of urinary alkalisers for the symptomatic treatment of uncomplicated UTIs. In conclusion, the current lack of evidence from randomised trials means that the safety and effectiveness of urinary alkalisers for managing symptoms of uncomplicated UTIs remain uncertain. Further research, particularly well-designed randomised controlled trials, is necessary to establish whether urinary alkalisers provide any clinical benefit in this context.
